prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a concrete, original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated in parallel) with an experimental programme that took fractional uncertainty to the 10^-18 level. The result is the most precisely controlled measurement system yet built, independently reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in laboratories on several continents and compared across fibre and satellite links. It is a discovery-level advance in what can be measured and how accurately, with consequences for tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, and the roadmap for redefining the SI second. It is the only shortlisted candidate with first-place support from two members and top-eight rankings from all eight, which suggests the case is broad rather than a reflection of one specialty. The two-person configuration is clean: Katori for the concept and first lattice clocks, Ye for driving systematics and coherence to the record regime.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with prior recognition: the 2005 prize covered the optical frequency comb on which these clocks depend, and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, which underlie competing ion clocks (Al+ and others) that also reached 10^-18. A committee could reasonably say the clock is an application of already honoured tools, or that credit for the best accuracy is shared with ion-clock and national-laboratory groups (PTB, NIST, SYRTE, and others) that two names cannot capture. The pending redefinition of the second also means the headline practical payoff has not yet arrived.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clear, nature-led surprise, with a sharp theory prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald) and a decisive experimental discovery (Jarillo-Herrero), and places lattice clocks fifth because of overlap with the 2005 comb prize and ion-clock credit.
responses.response: I agree that B022 is a striking discovery and that the theory-plus-experiment attribution is unusually clean, and I am not dismissing it. My reservation is maturity: several colleagues, including Eriksson, Johansson and Mehlig, note that the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated phases remain unsettled, and the discovery dates from 2018. Lattice clocks have a stable interpretation and have been confirmed by many independent groups over about two decades. On the overlap with the comb prize, I would say the comb is a tool for reading out an optical clock, whereas the new content is the magic-wavelength lattice and the control of systematics. Those are a different achievement. I keep B022 as my first alternative, but I would sooner wait for the physics to settle.

responses.point: Also ranks the lattice clock first, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and realised with strontium by both groups, but flags that the committee might see it as too close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control recognition and that the Katori versus Ye attribution for the first lattice clocks is not independently verified.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking and on the main risk. I would qualify the attribution worry: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the early Sr lattice clock, and Ye's group is the one that pushed accuracy and stability into the 10^-18 regime, so the two-person configuration reflects two different contributions, concept and realisation at record performance. I would not argue that the lattice clock is distinct from the ion clock in merit. The claim is only that the prize should be framed around the lattice concept so that it does not pretend to adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks. That framing should also answer the 2012 overlap objection, since the ion-control prize was awarded for manipulation of single quantum systems, not for this class of many-atom neutral-atom clock.

responses.point: Ranks the lattice clock only eighth, calling it important metrology but further from his own field, and notes that overlap with earlier frequency-comb and ion-trap prizes may reduce novelty and that the recognition is timely but not urgent.
responses.response: I understand that this sits far from electronic-structure theory, and that remoteness is a reason to test the case more carefully, not to discount it. I disagree that it is 'not urgent'. The 10^-18 level is where the clocks start to resolve gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and to provide a plausible path to redefining the second, and that is the kind of measurement-limited progress the Nobel Prize has recognised before. I do accept that novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 is the real debate and that it cannot be settled by counting top-three rankings. If the committee concludes the overlap is decisive, I would regard B046 as the better place to put atomic physics, though with a harder credit problem.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first and cold-atom lattices second, and places lattice clocks eighth, citing overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and ion-clock competition for credit.
responses.response: I take the point on competition from ion clocks and I would not word a citation so as to claim the lattice clock is categorically more accurate. On B044, I note that your own opening flags that Wallraff is not among the credited names and that the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize may overlap conceptually. Those two concerns together make B044 harder for me to put ahead of B036 now, as a three-name trio would leave out a decisive experimental group and the field has just been recognised. I would be willing to revisit this if you can argue concretely that circuit QED is a distinct discovery from the 2025 macroscopic quantum tunnelling work.

uncertainties: How far the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement about novelty, not a matter of evidence I can settle.

Whether ion-clock contributors (for example Al+ groups) and national-laboratory lattice-clock groups would be seen as having an equal claim that two names do not cover; I cannot verify detailed priority between the Katori and Ye groups for the first lattice clocks.
Timing relative to the redefinition of the SI second, which has not yet occurred and which I cannot verify.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile, I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder as a doctoral student, and Hall's comb-and-clock lineage at JILA is closely linked to Jun Ye's group, so a possible recusal question arises for B036; I have no documented personal, collaborative or institutional tie to Katori or Ye themselves. I am an atomic physicist at Lund, with documented Lund collaborators (Rippe, Walther, Kinos), WACQT and Deep Light Vision, none of whom appear among the shortlisted credited names. The committee should decide whether the Hall-lab connection warrants recusal on B036.
